clue.text: A dreamy way to heaven

parts.note: in Genesis the patriarch dreams of a stairway reaching up to heaven with angels on it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreamy' is not 'lovely' but literal: the way to heaven was seen in a dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical patriarch's dream showed a stairway linking earth and heaven, so the name of that vision is literally a way to heaven seen in a dream.

clue.text: The Thunderer

parts.note: the chief Roman god wielded the thunderbolt and was called Tonans, the thunderer

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Thunderer' is also the old nickname of The Times itself, the paper this puzzle ran in; here it is the Roman sky god.
explanation.definitionFit: The supreme Roman deity hurled thunderbolts and was worshipped under the title Tonans.

clue.text: For paddlers who prefer dry feet ?

definitions.text: For paddlers who prefer dry feet ?

parts.words: For paddlers who prefer dry feet
parts.note: paddlers suggests people wading at the seaside, but here they wield paddles in a small boat and stay dry

explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddlers' suggests children wading in the shallows; the paddles are the kind you row with, from inside a light boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A light boat propelled by paddles keeps its occupants out of the water, unlike wading.

clue.text: A creative literary gent of course !

definitions.meaning: someone who makes books, an author or publisher
at the racecourse, the man who takes bets

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the word is a maker of books; 'of course' points to the racecourse, where the same word means the man taking bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer produces volumes, while at the racecourse the same term names the person who takes bets and sets odds.

clue.text: Vulpine morning hide-out

parts.note: vulpine means fox-like; the fox hunts by night and lies up in its den by morning

explanation.walkthrough: Foxes are nocturnal, so morning is when one goes to ground in its den.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild animal's den, especially a fox's, is where it hides away during the day.

clue.text: One party's overhead act is quite legal

definitions.text: One party's overhead act is quite legal

parts.words: One party's overhead act is quite legal
parts.note: a legal deed made by one party only, its top edge cut straight (polled) rather than indented as for a two-party deed

explanation.walkthrough: A deed between two parties was cut with a wavy top edge (an indenture); a deed by one person had its top cut straight, 'polled', hence 'overhead'. It is the British way of changing one's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This legal instrument is executed by a single person, typically to change a name, and its paper was traditionally shaved even at the top.

clue.text: Introduced to little Mary

parts.note: little Mary is old British slang for the stomach, so food introduced to her has been swallowed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Mary' was an Edwardian euphemism for the stomach, from a J. M. Barrie play; 'introduced' looks social but means swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been consumed has been sent down to the stomach, known in old slang as little Mary.

clue.text: The really top people are used to such accommodation

definitions.text: The really top people are used to such accommodation

parts.words: The really top people are used to such accommodation
parts.note: the top people are royalty, who live in grand residences fit for a monarch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Really' hides the Latin-style 'royal': the truly top people live in royal homes.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes housing as grand and splendid as a royal residence.

clue.text: Not the husky North European variety

definitions.text: Not the husky North European variety

parts.words: Not the husky North European variety
parts.note: a husky sledge dog might come from Lapland, but this pet is a small pampered dog that sits on one's knee

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer and it looks like a Lapp dog, a hardy breed from Lapland; the actual pet is the tiny pampered kind carried on the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pampered pet that sits on its owner's knee is the opposite of a tough sledge dog.

clue.text: Peter has to go through the motions, just for show

parts.note: Peter Pan, the boy who never grew up
taken as written
to mime is to act out movements without words

explanation.surface: Someone named Peter just goes through the motions for appearances' sake.
explanation.walkthrough: PAN comes from Peter Pan, J. M. Barrie's play, itself a classic of the form; 'has' and 'just for' only link the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christmas stage entertainment with songs and slapstick is a kind of theatrical show.

clue.text: Crown one in Ireland's royal hill

indicators.note: the numeral for one is placed inside the name of the hill

parts.note: the Hill of Tara was the seat of the ancient High Kings of Ireland
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A coronation takes place on the ancient royal hill in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hill of Tara in County Meath was where Irish High Kings were crowned; I goes inside TARA.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled headband is a small ornamental coronet worn on the head.

clue.text: The packet from the North Sea

definitions.text: The packet from the North Sea

parts.words: The packet from the North Sea
parts.note: packet looks like a mail boat, but here it is a quantity of gas piped from North Sea fields and billed in units of heat

explanation.walkthrough: A 'packet' sounds like a boat or a parcel; North Sea gas was billed to British households in heat units.
explanation.definitionFit: British gas bills charged for North Sea gas in these units, each 100,000 British thermal units of heat.

clue.text: A continental type from the East End of London and Paris

indicators.text: from the East End of London
indicators.note: in the East End, Cockney speech mangles words, so the following letters come out rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A European turns up from London's East End and from Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: London and Paris are the decoy; only 'and Paris' is fodder, rearranged under the loose signal 'from the East End of London', Cockney speech being famous for mangling words.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Spain is a person from the Continent, as Britons call mainland Europe.

clue.text: Play false-pretending heartlessness perhaps

parts.note: in bridge or whist, failing to follow suit when able, such as claiming to have no hearts while holding one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessness' is not cruelty but having no cards in hearts; a player who discards while holding the suit led breaks the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games the term means failing to follow suit when one could, a breach of the rules.

clue.text: So venomous, six die

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral for six
to perish is to die

explanation.surface: Snakes so venomous that six people die.
explanation.definitionFit: Snake-like and spiteful, full of poison like an adder.

clue.text: When the sun has gone to rest

definitions.text: When the sun has gone to rest

parts.words: When the sun has gone to rest
parts.note: the dim period of evening light after sunset, a poetic Scots word for dusk

explanation.definitionFit: Twilight is the time after sunset before full darkness falls.

clue.text: She is bounteous to a degree

definitions.text: She is bounteous to a degree

parts.words: She is bounteous to a degree
parts.note: the Latin phrase means nourishing mother, a name for one's university, which grants a degree

explanation.walkthrough: 'To a degree' looks like 'somewhat' but means awarding a university degree; the Latin phrase means bounteous mother.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, literally nourishing mother, names the university or school from which one graduated.

clue.text: Whom the king delighted to honour

definitions.text: Whom the king delighted to honour

parts.words: Whom the king delighted to honour
parts.note: in the Book of Esther, Haman is made to honour Esther's cousin as 'the man whom the king delighteth to honour'

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase quotes Esther 6, where King Ahasuerus rewards Esther's cousin for foiling a plot.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Esther the Persian king chose to honour Esther's cousin, using exactly this biblical phrase.

clue.text: Super-charged particle that won the Derby

parts.note: hyper- means above or super
an ion is an atom carrying electric charge

explanation.surface: A turbocharged subatomic particle romps home at Epsom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Super-charged' looks like one word, but the hyphen splits it: super gives HYPER and 'charged particle' gives ION. The Derby is Britain's premier flat horse race, run at Epsom.
explanation.definitionFit: The colt of this name won the Epsom Derby in 1933 and became a great sire.

clue.text: Victoria's old flame

parts.note: an old flame suggests a former sweetheart, but here it is a dashing cavalry soldier of the Victorian age, a lady's romantic fancy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old flame' points at a lover of the queen; it is the kind of cavalryman Victorian girls swooned over.
explanation.definitionFit: A light-cavalry soldier in a showy uniform was the classic romantic heart-throb of Victorian times.

clue.text: Bob the runner seems amused

definitions.note: the definition describes the person who looks amused, a noun for someone grinning

parts.note: a bob was a shilling, abbreviated s
a miler is an athlete who runs the mile

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name but is old British slang for a shilling, written s in pre-decimal money.
explanation.definitionFit: One who looks amused wears a grin, so a grinning person fits.

clue.text: Takes the chair but loses the piano, as one does at home

indicators.note: the leading letter is lost from the word for chairing, leaving the rest

parts.note: to preside is to take the chair at a meeting
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A chairman who gives up his piano sits back at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing P from PRESIDES leaves the answer; 'the piano' sounds like an instrument, but means the musical marking p.
explanation.definitionFit: Living somewhere means making one's home there, which is what one does at home.

clue.text: Unruffled about publicity for Eine Kleine Nachtmusik ?

indicators.note: the word for calm goes around the advertisement, enclosing it

parts.note: serene means calm and unruffled
an ad is a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: Calm publicity for Mozart's famous night music.
explanation.walkthrough: Mozart's 'Eine Kleine Nachtmusik' ('a little night music') is a piece in this genre, so the question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozart's piece is an example of an evening musical composition of this genre.

clue.text: Producing Twang ?

parts.note: a twang is a quality of voice made through the nose

explanation.walkthrough: 'Twang' looks like a plucked string; it is the nasal tone of a voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A twangy voice is one sounded through the nose.

clue.text: Many appear in half-hose or rustic overalls

indicators.note: the letter for many goes inside the word for half-hose

parts.note: half-hose is an old term for socks
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: Lots of people show up in short stockings or farm workwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-hose' is an old term for socks, as opposed to full-length stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose outer garments of coarse linen were worn by farm labourers, the traditional countryman's working garb.

clue.text: Martian conduit ?

parts.note: Schiaparelli and Lowell thought they saw artificial waterways crossing the surface of Mars

explanation.walkthrough: Astronomers once believed straight lines on Mars were artificial waterways, the question mark admitting they were not.
explanation.definitionFit: An artificial watercourse; the supposed lines on Mars were translated as such.

clue.text: Old Macdonald's holding

parts.note: in the nursery song, Old Macdonald had an agricultural plot with animals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding' looks like gripping, but is an agricultural holding, the one in the nursery song.
explanation.definitionFit: A smallholding is land worked for crops and livestock, as in the children's song.

clue.text: What fools, those Roman coppers !

definitions.meaning: the as was a Roman copper coin, plural in -es

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' looks like police officers; the as was a bronze or copper Roman coin, whose plural looks like 'donkeys'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fools are called donkeys, and the Roman copper coin, the as, has the same plural form.

clue.text: The dances are unusually subdued

indicators.note: the letters of these words arranged in an unusual way, so they are rearranged

explanation.definitionFit: Someone humbled and restrained by a rebuke is cowed and quiet.

clue.text: Not a game for city bairns, but the glory that was Greece

definitions.text: Not a game for city bairns, but the glory that was Greece

parts.words: Not a game for city bairns, but the glory that was Greece
parts.note: the playground game of glass balls, as played by children of a Scottish town, is not meant; it is the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum

explanation.walkthrough: Elgin is a town in north-east Scotland, and bairns is Scots for children; the marbles meant are the Greek sculptures Lord Elgin brought to London, 'the glory that was Greece' quoting Poe.
explanation.definitionFit: These Parthenon sculptures, taken to Britain by Lord Elgin, embody the art of classical Greece.
